source.title_on_document: Exploring the Role of Generative Artificial Intelligence in Creative Thinking Processes: results from a preliminary study.

paper_design_summary: University students recruited during regular coursework read and analyzed a disciplinary text, with individual random assignment explicitly reported to AI access for the preparatory analysis/evaluation questions or to no digital support; the authors also call the design quasi-experimental (pp. 3–4, sections 2.1–2.2). Participants then produced a social media post, with AI access restricted to the preceding questions, and the post was assessed using a creative production rubric (pp. 3–6, sections 2.1–2.3). The paper compares the total rubric score across groups and also describes A.S.K. creative potential and its associations, and those of self-reported AI familiarity, with the same creative performance outcome (pp. 6–8, sections 3.2–3.5).

studies.label: AI-supported text analysis followed by an unaided creative social media post

assignment.what_was_assigned: Individual students to an experimental group allowed AI tools for the first two Analysis/Evaluation questions, or a control group completing the entire activity without digital support. Random assignment is explicitly stated despite the quasi-experimental label. The assignment method and sequence generation are not described.
assignment.quote: The sample, composed of university students, was randomly assigned to either an experimental group or a control group.
assignment.locator: p. 3, section 2.1 (Research Design). Conflicting quasi-experimental characterization: p. 1, Abstract; p. 3, section 2.1; pp. 9–10, section 5.

arms.name: Group A – with AI
arms.description: Allowed generative AI tools when answering the preparatory Analysis/Evaluation questions; this permission did not extend to the final Creation question (p. 3, section 2.1; p. 1, Abstract). The analyzed count is the N printed for creative performance in p. 6, Table 1.

arms.name: Group B – without digital tools
arms.description: Completed the entire activity without any digital support (p. 3, section 2.1). The analyzed count is the N printed for creative performance in p. 6, Table 1.

participants.exclusions: No participant exclusions or attrition flow are reported. The authors explicitly retained one Management Engineering Master’s student in the analyses (p. 4, section 2.2). Assignment-stage counts are not separately given, so n_randomized is left null; the group counts are taken from the outcome analysis (p. 6, Table 1).
participants.who: Convenience sample of university students recruited during regular coursework, mainly in Economics and Data Analysis or Business Economics. The sample is described as undergraduate, but the authors also state that one Management Engineering Master’s student was included and retained (p. 4, section 2.2).
participants.quote: The sample consisted of 56 undergraduate students, evenly distributed by gender, with a mean age of 21 years; approximately 80% of the participants were aged 21 or younger.
participants.locator: p. 4, section 2.2 (Sample); p. 6, Table 1 (28 analyzed in each arm); p. 1, Abstract (fifty-six students completed the creative task).

ai_tool.name_model: Generative AI tools; provider, product and model not stated.
ai_tool.how_used: Support for the preparatory text-analysis/evaluation questions only (p. 3, section 2.1). No model, prescribed prompts, interaction protocol, usage logs or exposure duration is specified. The discussion says the quality of interaction was not directly observable or standardized (p. 9, section 4). PsyToolkit and/or Google Forms are named as questionnaire platforms, not as the AI intervention (p. 4, section 2.3).

task.description: Read Matteo Minelli’s text “Tribal Economy: When Not Doing Becomes Abundance,” answer the preparatory analysis/evaluation questions, and then create a post for Instagram, X/Twitter or Facebook. The post could contain up to 800 characters, including a title/slogan, and had to creatively synthesize and reinterpret the ideas of an economy of abundance and not doing in contemporary society (pp. 3–5, sections 2.1 and 2.3).

outcomes.name: Total_Create: total creative production rubric score
outcomes.question: after_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Analytic rubric for the participant's social media post, comprising conceptual re-elaboration, originality and synthesis of the message, thematic relevance, and linguistic appropriateness and communicative tone. Each indicator is rated 0–3, with a maximum total of 12 points (pp. 5–6, section 2.3). Coded as human_raters for the rubric-based evaluation; the document does not identify the scorers, their expertise or number, whether they were blinded, or inter-rater reliability. This is the only creative performance outcome reported by experimental group (p. 6, section 3.2 and Table 1); no explicit primary-outcome designation is stated.

contrasts.reported: Group A – with AI: N = 28, Mean = 8.21, Std. Dev. = 1.97; Group B – without digital tools: N = 28, Mean = 7.64, Std. Dev. = 1.94. The text reports +0.57 points, p = .31, and Cohen’s d = 0.26. The higher mean for Group A was not statistically significant. The effect size is transcribed exactly as printed; no effect size or standard error has been computed.
contrasts.locator: p. 6, Table 1 and section 3.2 (Creative Performance Results); conclusion continues on p. 7. AI restriction to the preceding questions: p. 3, section 2.1; p. 1, Abstract.

outcomes.name: Conceptual re-elaboration (rubric indicator)
outcomes.question: after_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Ability to rework the text's concepts; this is not a count of elaboration or output length. Named as a separately rated indicator of the creative production rubric, on a 0–3 ordinal scale (pp. 5–6, section 2.3). Rater identity, expertise, number, blinding and reliability are not reported. Only the total rubric score is reported by group; no separate indicator means, uncertainty, effect size or hypothesis test is given (p. 6, section 3.2 and Table 1). Included because the methods explicitly say each indicator was rated. There is no separately reported contrast for this indicator. AI was restricted to the preceding analysis/evaluation questions (p. 3, section 2.1).

eligibility.reason: The procedural description explicitly states random assignment of students to AI access versus no digital support (p. 3, section 2.1), although the abstract and limitations call the design quasi-experimental. The analyzed sample is 56 people, with 28 per group (p. 4, section 2.2; p. 6, Table 1). A creative production rubric scores the social media posts, and a between-group total-score comparison is reported (pp. 5–6, section 2.3 and Table 1). AI access was restricted to the analytical questions preceding the creative post, so the eligible question is after_ai (p. 1, Abstract; p. 3, section 2.1). The randomization-label conflict and setting details require audit, but the explicit random-assignment statement supports inclusion under the codebook.

one_line_finding: Students allowed AI during the preceding analysis scored 8.21 (SD 1.97, n = 28) versus 7.64 (SD 1.94, n = 28) on the subsequent unaided creative post, with no statistically significant difference (p = .31; printed Cohen’s d = 0.26; p. 6, Table 1 and section 3.2).
open_questions: How was random assignment implemented, and why do the abstract and limitations describe the design as quasi-experimental despite the explicit random-assignment statement (p. 3, section 2.1; pp. 9–10, section 5)?

Was the activity administered during ordinary coursework, in a supervised research session, or remotely? field_rct is a provisional setting classification based on the coursework context; recruitment during coursework and online questionnaire collection are stated, but the assessment venue is not (pp. 3–5, sections 2.1–2.3).
Which generative AI tools were available, how much were they used, and how was the restriction to the preparatory questions implemented (p. 3, section 2.1; p. 9, section 4)?

Who applied the creative production rubric, were scorers human and blinded, what was their expertise, and was scoring reliability assessed? These details are absent from the rubric description (pp. 5–6, section 2.3).

Can the A.S.K. gender table be clarified? Its Average row prints Male n = 20, Female n = 15, and Total n = 37 (p. 7, Table 2); the gender cells and printed total are inconsistent. This table was not used to replace the creative-performance sample count.
notes: Read the entire markdown conversion and extracted the text of all PDF pages, including references; there are no appendices in the saved PDF. All recorded numerical findings were checked against PDF text. No supplement, study data/code URL, preregistration, sample reuse, participant-country statement, or task duration is reported. The saved document is dated 2026 in its journal header and copyright; the search record and filenames label it 2025. The field_rct setting code is provisional because coursework recruitment is explicit but the administration setting is not; randomization is coded from the procedural statement rather than the quasi-experimental label. Human_raters is the closest rubric-evaluation code, but the scorer type and qualifications are not explicitly stated and need confirmation. Immediate timing reflects the sequence within the described activity; no later session or numeric delay is stated. The total score and its named, individually rated rubric indicators are listed as five outcome records; only the total has a reported group contrast. No separate component results were invented. A.S.K. scores are described as creative potential and reported by gender/performance band and in a correlation with the post score, without an AI-condition comparison or a stated timing relative to AI exposure (p. 5, section 2.3; pp. 7–8, sections 3.3 and 3.5). They are therefore not coded as an additional AI-effect outcome. DIGCOMP is self-reported familiarity; its descriptive results and correlations with the same creative score are not separate creative-output outcomes (pp. 5–6, sections 2.3 and 3.1; p. 8, section 3.4). The comprehension questions have no scored result reported, and no across-person diversity measure is reported. Standard errors, confidence intervals, and a numerical between-group test statistic are not given for Total_Create; the printed mean difference and Cohen’s d are retained without recalculation.
